pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4), PROCEDURAL: using a dichotomous (branching yes/no) classification key to identify minibeasts — 'Does it have legs?' → 'How many?' → 'Does it have wings?' — and grasping WHY a fixed order of questions lets you identify a creature you've never seen.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' — explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name living things in local and wider environments.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-LS4 / classification practices (using tools and reasoning to identify and group organisms).
• Operational details — a key is a PROCEDURE: each question must split the remaining set into two, using an observable, unambiguous feature. Teach children both to FOLLOW a key and to BUILD one (choosing good splitting questions). The power idea: a key works on unfamiliar creatures because it asks about features, not names. Start with real specimens/photos and a small key (4-6 creatures).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): follows a given branching key to identify 4 minibeasts. Tier B (age 8): writes a yes/no question that separates two groups (e.g. 'Does it have six legs?'). Tier C (age 9): explains why a set order of questions works even for a creature never seen before, and builds a small key.
bestPractices: Have children both FOLLOW and BUILD keys — building forces them to choose good splitting questions and reveals the underlying logic.
Insist each question uses an observable, unambiguous feature that splits the set into two (avoid vague 'is it pretty?').
Start small (4-6 real specimens or photos) and grow the key gradually.
Make the narrowing visible — candidates eliminated at each step — so children see how questions reduce possibilities.
Draw out the big idea: a key works on unfamiliar creatures because it asks about features, not names.
keyRepresentations: A live candidate row that shrinks as questions are answered.
A build-a-key tree with forks the child fills in.
Feature-based splitting-question cards ('Does it have six legs?').
commonMisconceptions: 'A key identifies by name/appearance' — it works by asking about observable features, which is why it handles unknown creatures.
'Questions can be in any order' — the order structures the narrowing; a good key splits systematically.
'Any question will do' — a useful question must cleanly divide the remaining set into two.
'If I don't recognise the creature I can't identify it' — the key's whole point is identifying the unfamiliar.
Choosing subjective questions ('is it scary?') that don't reliably split organisms.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4), this procedural topic teaches children to use a dichotomous (branching yes/no) classification key to identify minibeasts, and crucially to understand WHY a fixed order of feature-based questions can identify a creature they have never seen before, as long as that creature is one the key includes. It aligns to UK DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things) and loosely supports US NGSS life-science practices of observing and comparing traits. Learners both FOLLOW a given key and BUILD their own, choosing good splitting questions. The core insight: a key works on creatures you do not recognise, provided they are in the key, because it asks about observable features, not names. (The classic question 'Does it have six legs?' is used to separate insects from spiders in a small minibeast set, not as a full definition of 'insect'.)

activities.title: Identify a mystery minibeast by walking a key
feedback: If you name the creature by sight first and only use the key to justify your guess, cover the answers and read/answer each question aloud in order before naming anything — following the path is the rule, not the guess.

If you take the wrong branch after miscounting a feature (e.g. counting a spider as six legs), slow down: count each leg on the specimen or photo before answering. The key only works if you read the feature correctly.
Prompt to check understanding: 'You reached spider. Which answer along the way ruled out insect?'
Prompt for transfer: 'I hand you a creature you have never seen, but it is one of the creatures in our key. Why does going through the questions in order help more than just guessing?'
activities.rationale: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things. Making the elimination visible — candidates dropping away at each yes/no — is a proposed way to help children feel why ordered feature-questions narrow the field, which is the conceptual heart of a dichotomous key.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment.
Dichotomous keys identify organisms through a fixed sequence of paired either/or questions about observable features, enabling identification of unfamiliar specimens.
learnerActions: Use a small branching key (4-6 creatures) to identify a minibeast you cannot see all at once — you can only answer questions about it.
Trace the ONE mystery creature: 'Does it have legs?' → yes, so the legless candidates (e.g. worms, snails) drop out of a row of possibilities.
Continue the SAME creature: 'Six legs?' → no, eight; the insects fall away, leaving the arachnids. 'Two body parts?' → yes; the last card flips to reveal a spider.

Now, as a separate task, work through the key for at least four different minibeasts (e.g. ant, spider, woodlouse, snail): for EACH one, start at the top question and follow the branch that ITS own answers point to until you reach a name — different creatures take different branches.
For each identification, name which single answer along the way ruled out a wrong group (e.g. which answer ruled out 'insect').
activities.intendedInsight: A key identifies by asking about observable features in a set order; each answer narrows the remaining possibilities, so an ordered sequence of questions can pin down even a creature you have never met, as long as it is one of the creatures the key includes.

activities.title: Build your own key and test it
feedback: If you write a question that isn't a clean yes/no or doesn't separate the groups, test it on two known creatures — if everyone answers the same way, push toward countable/observable features (legs, wings, body parts).
Counterexample prompt: 'Could your question "Does it have wings?" put a wingless ant in the wrong group? How would you fix the key?'
If you can't say why order matters, walk one creature top-to-bottom and notice how each answer narrows the possibilities; starting in the middle skips the narrowing.

In a build-and-test tool, a question that fails to split the group cleanly can be flagged immediately so you can see what makes a good splitting question; this live flag is one helpful option, not the only way to learn it.
activities.rationale: Having children build as well as follow keys makes them choose good splitting questions, which surfaces the logic that a useful question must cleanly divide the remaining set using an observable feature. Testing the key on creatures from the set that the user does not already recognise shows how the tool handles the unfamiliar. Trying a creature from outside the set shows that a key can only name creatures it includes, and that a key can be extended with new branches.
sourceClaims: Dichotomous keys identify organisms through a fixed sequence of paired either/or questions about observable features, enabling identification of unfamiliar specimens.
learnerActions: Take a set of six minibeasts and build your own branching key, choosing the yes/no question at each fork.

Write questions that use an observable, unambiguous feature that cleanly splits the remaining group into two. For example, 'Does it have six legs?' separates insects from spiders in this set (yes: the six-legged insects / no: the eight-legged spiders, plus any other legged creatures without six legs, such as a woodlouse with 14 legs).
Test each question on two known creatures: do they give different answers? If a woodlouse and an ant give the same answer, that question won't split them — revise it.
Avoid subjective or vague questions ('Is it scary?', 'Is it pretty?', 'Is it big?') because different people answer them differently for the same creature.

Swap keys with a partner and use their key to identify creatures from their set without being told the names, fixing any fork where a creature gets stuck or mis-sorted. Then run a creature that is NOT in the set through a key: notice that it gets stuck or lands on a wrong name, because a key can only name creatures it includes. Extend the key by adding a new question and end point for it.
activities.intendedInsight: Building a key forces you to choose good splitting questions: each must have a clear yes/no answer and genuinely divide the remaining set, revealing the underlying logic of why a key is reliable.

activities.title: Reasoning practice: order and choice of questions
feedback: If you pick a question that both creatures would answer the same way, note that it does not separate them — look for a feature where they differ.
If you think any question can come first, show how starting in the middle skips earlier narrowing; the order structures how the possibilities shrink.

These recognition and ordering tasks check reasoning about key logic, but they do not by themselves require you to construct and traverse a working key — pair them with the follow and build activities.
activities.rationale: Selecting and ordering splitting questions targets the misconceptions that 'any question will do' and 'order doesn't matter'. Recognition and ordering tasks assess reasoning but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a working key.
learnerActions: Given two minibeasts, choose which of several questions best splits them apart, and explain why the others fail.
Put a set of jumbled key steps into a sensible order so the questions narrow systematically.
Explain in your own words why a fixed order of questions helps you identify a creature you have never seen (as long as it is in the key), rather than just guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the best splitting question and ordering questions deliberately both depend on the same idea: good questions use clear, observable features and each one narrows the set.

constraints: Each question in a key must use an observable, unambiguous feature that splits the remaining set into two; avoid subjective questions ('is it pretty/scary?').
Start small (4-6 real specimens or photos) and grow the key gradually so the narrowing stays visible.
Draw out the big idea explicitly: a key works on creatures you do not recognise, as long as the key includes them, because it asks about features, not names.
Following a pre-made or tappable key is more passive; the deeper learning comes from traversing and especially building the branches. Use a tappable/reveal diagram as a scaffold, not the end goal.

Recognition-only tasks (multiple-choice, matching, ordering jumbled steps) assess reasoning about key logic but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a working key; include a build-and-test activity.

A 20-questions style dialogue can model the narrowing logic and is a legitimate alternative, but it makes the elimination less visible than a representation that shows candidates dropping away; treat it as a complement.
Reading features correctly (e.g. counting legs, spotting body parts) is a prerequisite — if a child miscounts, reteach insect/non-insect features before concluding the key is at fault.
Treat 'Does it have six legs?' as a feature that separates insects from spiders in the given set, not as a complete definition of an insect.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D interactive as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing' and asserted a quiz 'can't let the child walk a live branch'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped statements about affordances (recognition tasks don't require construction; dialogue makes elimination less visible) rather than universal claims.

The 'each question halves the possibilities' phrasing in the legacy design notes is an idealisation — a key question splits the remaining set into two groups but not necessarily into equal halves. Activities say 'narrows/splits into two' rather than 'halves'.
The live-recolour/grey-out and drag-into-tree interactions are retained as optional concrete examples of how elimination and building can be made visible, not as mandatory mechanisms.
The original NGSS 3-LS4 alignment is retained in the summary alongside the KS2 Y4 reference.

The worked mystery walk uses 'worms' as a legless example while the four-creature diagnostic set is ant/spider/woodlouse/snail; legless examples illustrate the wider candidate pool and need not all appear in the specific diagnostic set.
'Does it have six legs?' is kept as a question that separates insects from spiders in this small set rather than as a universal definition of 'insect'.

probeDeeper: 'You reached "spider". Which answer along the way ruled out "insect"?'
'Test your new question on the woodlouse AND the ant — do they give different answers? If not, it won't split them.'
'I hand you a creature you've never seen. Why does going through the questions in order help more than just guessing?'
'Could your question "does it have wings?" put a wingless ant in the wrong group? How would you fix the key?' (counterexample forcing a robust feature)
assess.correctAnswer: The child starts at the first question of the key and answers each yes/no in order, following the branch its answer points to, until they reach a name — correctly identifying at least four minibeasts. When asked to extend the key, they write a question with a clear yes/no answer that genuinely separates the groups (e.g. 'Does it have six legs?' → yes: insect / no: not) and place it at a sensible branch point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Guesses the creature by sight first, then uses the key only to justify the guess — doesn't actually follow the branching
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover the answers and require them to read and answer each question aloud in order before naming anything. Make following-the-path the rule, not the guess.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the minibeast before reaching that point in the key; skips questions; jumps branches

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers a key question wrongly because they miscount or mis-observe the feature (e.g. counts a spider as 6 legs)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slow down the observation step: count and touch each leg before answering. The key only works if the feature is read correctly — reteach the insect/non-insect features if needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Takes the wrong branch after miscounting legs/body parts; ends at the wrong name

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes a splitting question that isn't a clean yes/no, or that doesn't actually separate the groups ('Is it scary?', 'Is it big?')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test their question on two known creatures: does everyone answer the same way? Push toward countable/observable features (legs, wings, body parts) with a definite yes/no.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Extension question is subjective or ambiguous; two children could answer it differently for the same creature

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't see why order matters — jumps around the key or thinks any question can come first
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that each answer NARROWS the possibilities; starting in the middle skips the narrowing. Walk one creature top-to-bottom to feel the funnel.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts in the middle of the key, or can't say why a set order helps with an unknown creature

responseLevels.gap: Guesses creatures by sight and can't follow the branching, or can't produce a yes/no splitting question at all.
responseLevels.full: Works the key systematically top-to-bottom to identify four+ minibeasts, authors a clean feature-based yes/no question that genuinely splits the groups and places it sensibly, AND explains that ordered questions narrow down an unknown creature — transferring the tool, not just running it.
responseLevels.partial: Follows the key to identify the given creatures but mechanically — can't explain why order matters, or writes a splitting question that is vague or doesn't cleanly separate the groups.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a simple branching key and four minibeasts to identify (e.g. ant, spider, woodlouse, snail). Work through the key out loud for each creature and tell me what each one is. Then I'll give you a creature that ISN'T on the key — make up a yes/no question that would split the insects from the spiders, and show me where it would go.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child WORK the key reveals whether they use it systematically — starting at the top, taking one question at a time, following the branch — or whether they jump straight to a guess and only use the key to confirm. Asking them to author a splitting question shows whether they understand a key is built from features with clean yes/no answers, not vague ones. Do not ask them to describe how a key works; set the task and watch the procedure.
